en: Kanchoro and brave Kyyaz
Stood bristling at each other,
Wrangling angrily.
With shouts that split the sky,
They plunged into an uproar,
Into a tumult
From which no man could turn away.
Darkening with rage,
Kyyaz stood shouting,
“Great host of the Kara-Jediger,
Come, every one of you!” he cried.
“Great host of the Kara-Jediger,
My people, heed the words I speak!
Go forth to the borders of our land!
See what war is and what peace is—
My people, witness it for yourselves!
Once we were the forty tribes of the Kyrgyz,
Dwelling along the Ala-Too.
While lion Manas lived,
No enemy could scatter us with war cries.
At the frontier stood brave Manas,
Coiling like a dragon;
When they beheld the hero’s might,
Even the Chinese in Kakan were roused.
The sevenfold Ala-Too
He won as our homeland through valor;
The Kyrgyz of these towering mountains
He gathered and forged into a nation.
By fighting, he brought them prosperity;
By building, he gave them homes;
The scattered, wandering Kyrgyz
He labored to make one people.
The towering Ala-Too
He made a refuge for the Kyrgyz.
While mighty Manas lived,
He turned and struck the Afghans;
What people in the mountain folds escaped unharmed?
While formidable Manas stood,
We raided Kunjut and took it daily;
We opened a road into India,
Breaking through stone to make the way;
We attacked many lands.
We struck Jet-Kayt and conquered it seven times;
How could Jet-Kayt have remained
Unscathed by us Kyrgyz?
In those days the peerless hero Manas—
Whose dwelling was great Talas—
Drove white deer home and made them cattle,
And filled every battlefield with tumult.
My father Agysh often used to say:
“Since life was first created, one like Manas
Has never come among the Kyrgyz, nor anywhere
In all the world.”
When the Chinese host engulfed the land,
When all faced utter ruin together,
“Manas was our stronghold,” he would say,
“Manas took his keen steel
Into his hand,” he would say.
“Throughout the whole world he raised
A mighty commotion,” he would say;
“From the infidels he rescued
The descendants of the few Kyrgyz
And brought them home,” he would say.
“When he turned to face the foe,
He was like a written decree,” he would say;
“Not only to the Kyrgyz, but for all time,
Khan Manas, now gone to eternity,
Became a father,” he would say.
“To the Kyrgyz, whose saddles sagged,
He became a support,” he would say.
“From age to age, at some destined time,
Not only for the Kyrgyz but for all time,
He became a fruit of blessing,” he would say.
“From age to age, at some destined time,
Brave Manas, gone to eternity,
Would be needed again,” he would say.
“To those who endured affliction,
To those left beneath the scorching sun,
For the multitude brave Manas
Became a sheltering poplar,” he would say.
“Always and forever,
The wretched Kyrgyz cannot bring down the wolf,
Nor bear to see the son who does;
Khan Manas, who guided them,
Was their shared seed, like white wheat,
Their rallying cry, like a white stallion,
Sharing whatever they acquired,
Brothers in faith, sharing even death,
Of one arm and one ancestry,
Of one wish and one blessing,
The issue of a single stallion,
The foals of a single man.
Take careful heed of this:
Sharing one nest with Manas
Was Shygay Khan in former times.
Let us tell the tale from its beginning:
Chynkojo, who stirred up strife,
Was that same Shygay’s son.
Two words can destroy a people;
He was a cunning rogue who shook whole nations.
The one who sowed strife among the multitude
Was truly that accursed oath-breaker.
Yesterday sorcery descended upon his waist,
And he stirred foul strife among his people.
Yesterday Manas’s son Semetey
Was made an enemy of his own people;
He came harboring evil designs
Against that lion Khan Semetey.
May that Kojo never prosper—
Chynkojo, destroyer of nations,
May there never be another like him.
Yesterday they bound their pinewood spears,
And made war against the bloodthirsty hero;
He scattered their days of happiness,
That glib-tongued, fawning slave,
And fled toward my elder brother Toltoy.
The clans camped along the valley,
And he greatly inflamed the quarrel;
It became a feud unto death.
He became khan of the Jediger,
Convulsing and destroying the people;
Spreading slander and ruining the nation,
The disheveled Kojo came to no good.
Shuffling about day and night,
He whispered and incited Toltoy:
“A slave has caught and mounted
The black horse no lasso could touch;
Old Bakay has entered the palace,
White as a swan;
He has spoken twisting words,
Words inspired by a white devil;
He has trampled the waters of Jeti-Özön;
More than that—even your
Wife has been seized,” he said,
Slandering them to brave Toltoy.
Thus Kojo corrupted and incited him,
Speaking words that split all apart;
My simplehearted uncle Toltoy
He corrupted by distorting his words.
Chynkojo was truly depraved:
Among the Jediger of Jeti-Özön
He stirred them into a frenzy,
Turning their elder into an enemy
And corrupting all the people.
Once the Jediger were corrupted,
They mounted stallions from the tethering line,
And took saddle blankets from the ground;
They became an army beneath whose weight the earth sagged,
Not a small host, but a multitude.
Raising a gray-and-white banner,
They filled every quarter with uproar;
Without hesitation they crossed the ridge,
For the woman he was to marry—
To seize her back,
They quarreled with Semetey.
They felled pines and made troughs,
Heaping gathered grass like mountains;
“I shall take your wife,” he said,
And laid a claim against Semetey.
Because of what had happened,
Because of Chynkojo,
They fell upon one another and fought,
And a terrible conflict arose.
Chynkojo was treacherous;
Because of Chynkojo,
Because of that true villainy,
The noble Kyrgyz clashed,
Facing one another in battle.
The nation was shattered and its finest men died;
Through Chynkojo’s cruelty,
So many heroes died here.
Many lofty plane trees were cut down;
A massacre swept the land,
Silencing the necks of many maidens’ champions.
Many kinds of warriors died,
And countless others also perished.
My uncle Toltoy died,
And that noble man entered
The true abode from which none return.
That wicked Kojo Khan died,
And every soul who followed him died.
Chynkojo, that son of Shygay,
Met a dreadful counterstroke;
Because Kojo caused it,
In that counterstroke my uncle,
Noble Toltoy, died.
A flood ruins the mountain valleys;
Among a people, Kanchoro,
A warrior like you brings ruin.
Wind lays waste the land;
A fickle-hearted, fork-tongued man
Like you destroys a nation.
I traced the tale through its traditions,
And questioned those who knew;
From gray-bearded elders
I heard all this,
From those who had lived long lives.
Semetey took you in,
Calling you a legacy left by the noble dead,
And made you his little brother.
For your feast he slaughtered ninety beasts
And named you the valiant Kanchoro.
When you were an infant,
Though you were merely a waif,
He himself raised you.
So that your heart might grow rich,
He cut fat from the choicest meat and fed you;
So that you might become a special kinsman,
His mother Kanykey let you suck
At both her pure breasts.
When you sucked Kanykey’s left breast,
Black blood came forth.
“This suckling will become an enemy,”
His mother Kanykey cried in anguish.
“He will never be kin—let him go!
At heart he is an enemy by birth;
Slaughter this wretch!” she said.
But the panther was magnanimous,
He would not heed malicious words
And disobeyed his mother Kanykey.
Though your tongue sounds gentle,
You will never mend, Kanchoro;
At heart you are an enemy to the end.
Understand the wisdom of my words;
My precious one, my friend,
Heed what I say.
Why should we provoke the blessed gray-maned hero
And bring harm upon ourselves?
Lay down your anger, Kanchoro;
Come, let us depart safely to the borderlands.
Can a full-grown warrior
Prosper after defiling another’s salt?
Can there ever be another
Who wrecks a nation and corrupts its people?
Understand the wisdom of my words;
Do not leave your people destitute—
My noble friend, heed what I say!
From this hero Semetey
The lands of Jylgyn and Keng-Kol will remain,
And from him the white-capped Kyrgyz nation will remain;
The wretched will join these deeds into songs,
And if tomorrow the new generation
Should seek rest, it will stir up strife.
They will bind their pinewood spears
And wage war with hatred fixed in their hearts.
Think on this, Kanchoro:
To our right are the Russians,
On your flank are the Chinese,
Before you stand the riflemen;
Many enemies are waiting
To contend with us.
Why should we fight to the bitter end
Against this deeply rooted gray wolf?
Come, let us leave, Jediger.
If word that the Kyrgyz are slaughtering one another
Should reach the Chinese,
